utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 3rd of October. My greetings to everybody in the courtroom. The Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people helping us. I believe that Defence wanted to say something. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very sorry to be taking up court time but I'll just be two minutes with your permission to say something with respect to the 30th of December 2006 ruling of yours. It is a ruling about the manner in which documents are admitted or rather exhibits. Now, the deadlines are set for the reactions of the parties for the IC list, and witness list, once it is tendered and according to that, the Prosecution on Monday, that is to say the day before yesterday, tabled a request with respect to expert witness Miller. And yesterday, we were supposed to reply or, rather, oppose the proposal, but, Your Honours, quite simply we didn't have time to do that. And we don't wish to not take up this opportunity. So with the Trial Chamber's permission, could you please extend the deadline until tomorrow so that we can do that in good time tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after discussing the matter, is granting you this additional time. This is the first time and until now everything worked well. It so happens that this time you had to face this problem. Therefore, you are granted this extra time. And I believe Mr. Registrar has to give a few IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One of the parties have submitted list of objections to documents tendered by the OTP through Witness Nicholas J. Miller. The list admitted by 4D shall be given IC number 675. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now going to bring the witness in. He's been granted protective measures, but first let's lower the blinds. Regarding the timing, as was the case for the previous witness, the Prosecution will have two hours, and then the Defence teams will have three hours, that is 30 minutes each, and they can decide on the way they want to use that time. Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. It's possible that the direct examination will be less than the two hours that's been allotted but we appreciate the Court's willingness to give us that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Well, if you need less time and if the Defence needs this time, we might be able to stop earlier tomorrow, around 12.00 or 12.30. We might not need to sit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. Let me first check that you can hear me in Spanish. If this is so, please tell me you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do hear you very well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, you've been granted protective measures upon request by your government which accounts for the presence of the representative of the Spanish government in the courtroom. There will be face distortion and your name will not be revealed outside this courtroom. You were given a pseudonym, or you will be given it in a few minutes but for the transcript, can you first state your name, first name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And are you still working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted), have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare to tell the truth and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Some explanations as to the way the hearing is going to unfold. First of all, you're going to be given a pseudonym sheet. I don't know which number was given to you but it is stated on it and you'll write today's date and you'll sign this document, please. You will be DW --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it just occurs to me it's not quite clear, although the blinds are gone down are we still in open session? Because we don't appear to have gone into closed session and the witness has said his name. I am not quite sure what the technical position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I have written an order already for redaction. It's going to be taken out of the transcript. Please write your name and sign.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can I have a number for this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This document shall be given Exhibit number IC 676. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted), I wanted to give you some explanations as to the way your testimony is going to be given. You will have to answer in a few moments the questions put by the Prosecution based on written statements or on documents that will be provided to you. The Prosecutor told us that it should take under two hours. After this, you will be asked questions either by the Defence counsel themselves or by the accused. It's true the questions deal with technical matters or with personal contacts. You have judges in front of you. They too may ask questions of you at any time. If you fail to understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate. Ask the person asking you to rephrase the question. Every ninety minutes we have a 20 minute break to change the tapes and for everybody to have a rest and your testimony is scheduled over two days, today and tomorrow. Today, we'll sit until 12.30, we'll resume at 2.30 until 5.00 and tomorrow we'll start again at 9.00 and it may than we'll have to work at 2.30 again but we'll see whether we can finish before. If at any time you want to address the Court, do so, please. I will give you the floor. So this is in a very general way the way the hearing is going to take place. I remind you that we are in open session. If at any time anybody puts a question that is likely to reveal the identity of the witness, please ask for private session before doing so, in order to avoid any problem. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness, Witness DW.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that a procedure has been required by the Trial Chamber in respect of witnesses whose statements are going to be tendered under Rule 92 ter. I have a summary of the witness's testimony that I'm prepared to read as an introduction to his evidence. However, it's my belief that at least part of this needs to be read in private session because if I read it in public session, it could lead to the disclosure of the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, witness, have you previously provided on two occasions written statements to the Office of the Prosecutor here at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you recall if the first statement you gave was in October of 1997 and then the second one was more recently, in July of 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to the more recent statement in July of 2007. At the time that you provided that statement, did you answer the questions truthfully and to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And your providing a statement, the answers that you gave, were they provided freely and with no coercion or pressure exerted on you by anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Completely free in my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of the interview, sir, was your statement then read back to you in the language that you could understand so that you could confirm that the English version of it was correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the statement that you gave, the English version, did you then sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you recall if you put your initials on each page of that statement and also the annex of documents that was attached to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you go to binder -- one of the binders, I know you have three of them there, and I promise you we are not going to look at all the documents that are in them, there is a binder B, B3. It is 3 of 3. List B, binder 3 of 3. And if I take you to the very back of that, you'll see a document that's at tab number 10287. 10287. Which is the exhibit number, Mr. President. Witness, are you looking at -- is this the statement that you -- that we've been talking about, given by you in July of 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you see your signature and your initials on the English version of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you travelled here to The Hague a few days ago, and you had an opportunity to meet with me and also my colleague, Mr. Longone, in order to review your statement and the relevant documents, is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in going through that statement here over the last few days, are there any corrections that you wanted to make to the statement? Is there anything in it that you consider to be incorrect that needs to be fixed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No. I don't think there are any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, there was one issue which I believe you wanted to clarify a bit, and I'll direct you to paragraphs 12 to 15 of your statement. This relates to the question of Croatian army forces in your area of responsibility, and if you would like to clarify this issue for us, Witness, now is your opportunity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I have to underline what the actual statement says, to wit, I wanted -- I'm talking about the initial statement before the second and last one, because in the July statement, in my July statement, there are opinions and data different from those included in my statement of 1997. At that time, three years on from my return from Bosnia, I was asked to make a statement on the facts, but I was not given documents, but, sir, none of the documents which the Madrid Task Force had drafted in the area three years before. I was asked about facts, I was asked about the presence of the Croat army in my area of responsibility and I said that there was none. In July 2007, during my statement, I was in fact provided with plenty of documents from SpaBat and from the Madrid chain of command in which it was obvious that there were elements of the HV army in my area of responsibility. So I wanted to make it clear that the 1997 statement and what I said in it was due to the fact that I did not have that datum fresh in my mind. And so in -- I wanted to make clear that elements of the HV army was in fact not relevant for my daily duties. That's why perhaps I did not remember their presence. So my units did not talk about units of the HV rather. Rather it talked about a few isolated individuals and apparently the units were deployed in areas which we did not visit regularly. Most of the reports arriving at SpaBat are in fact reports from military personnel or from people from other detachments or battalions but not from my own battalion. This is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, now, having now made that clarification, are you prepared to accept as accurate and truthful all of the other information that's contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I have a small group of documents, then, that I'd like to show you over the next hour or so, that relate to some of the issues and the topics that are mentioned by you in your statement. And let me ask you this: During the past few days that you've been here in The Hague, with the Office of the Prosecutor, did you also have an opportunity to review the various Spanish Battalion reports that you've already referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity specifically to review the reports and the documents that are specifically referred to in your witness statement? And did you put your initials on all of those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The first of the documents, Witness, that I'd like to take you to, and what I've done is to arrange them simply in chronological order so that they cover roughly the time of your mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I guess I should say this for the -- before we start. Can you tell us when approximately you and the unit that you were attached to, when you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically the area of Mostar and Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: We arrived around the 23rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were attached to a unit that was tasked with various duties by the commander of the Task Force. Could you tell us just in general what were the responsibilities of the unit that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: The general mission of the UNPROFOR units were to protect humanitarian aid, to guarantee that humanitarian aid arrived where it had to arrive. That's to say to -- the organisations directed us to. Alongside that, our task force gave protection to and escort, rather, to convoys for the exchange of wounded people or prisoners. We also mediated between the parties to promote -- promote agreements between the parts in conflict with a view to reducing violence and making life, conditions, for all affected easier. We also provided medical assistance and aid to people wounded in the field. We provided medical assistance also by providing drugs or plasma to the hospitals in need of that. So this was our mission in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the unit, the specific unit that you were attached to, where did it have its main headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: My battalion's headquarters was in Dracevo and we had fixed detachments so to speak in East Mostar and another one in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a question or two about that. At what point in time did your unit establish a fixed detachment in East Mostar? Was that from the very beginning of your deployment or did that happen later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: From the beginning of our deployment, we had a permanent patrol in East Mostar but it was only later when we actually had a base. The patrol that was permanently in East Mostar lived in their own vehicle actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the patrol was there 24 hours a day living in their armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then at roughly what point in time, if you can say, did the unit actually establish a place, a detachment, in East Mostar? Do you recall what month approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I take it you are talking about a base, a physical, fixed base in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Towards the end of November, beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that from the very beginning, your unit had a physical presence in East Mostar of 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Permanently, from the moment we arrived to the moment we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what about West Mostar? Did the unit that you were attached to have personnel deployed or detached in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: In West Mostar, we had to patrol daily but not on the basis of 24 hour, around-the-clock patrol. We had a patrol during the day. The patrol entered West Mostar in the morning because a distance being short, they came back for lunch to our base, and then they went back in the afternoon. So in West Mostar, we only had a permanent base or we only managed to get one by the month of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to put a follow-up question in order to save time. The Prosecutor asked you whether the SpaBat had a unit in Mostar, either Mostar west or East Mostar. There is a question I have never asked, but I'm going to ask of you. If there is a conflict between two parties, the HVO and the ABiH, through evidence we have received we know that there is a front line that goes along this famous boulevard between the two parties. How can you explain that the SpaBat did not position themselves on the front line, since there were cease-fire agreements, there are examples in the past, in the history of the UN, in which there are forces that are put in between or forces that are positioned between the warring factions. Think of Lebanon. How can you explain that in Mostar, whilst there was a series of cease fires, we have had evidence about this, nobody thought of positioning the UNPROFOR between the warring parties? Do you have an opinion, or an explanation? Was this question ever envisaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I perhaps have no explanations to give. The UNPROFOR mandate was crystal clear, to protect humanitarian aid, with clear rules of engagement that prevented us from using force except in the case of legitimate self defence. UNPROFOR was never an intervention force. We were not patrolling the confrontation line. That was not part of our mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, the patrols sent out vehicles either to West Mostar or to East Mostar, but not on the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. We escorted humanitarian aid convoys. That was our specific UNPROFOR mandate. We protected convoys carrying or ferrying wounded people, and even transported wounded people or prisoners should the situation require us to do this. But we never actually deployed ourselves in between the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in addition to protecting and escorting the convoys, did your battalion not have an observation mission to carry out, which has nothing to do with protecting the convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We had an observation mission as a task derived from our general mandate. When we arrived, there was an agreement between the two parties which was later known as the Medjugorje memorandum. And in the case of Mostar there was an agreement to reduce shooting and shelling and not to undertake military operations near or around hospitals. Hence, the East and West Mostar patrols had as one of their duties to count the number of explosions or the shell impacts coming from the other side or arriving at the actual side. This was one of the tasks that we undertook as part of our observation mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answers. I apologise, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Could the witness please be asked whether he's aware of the agreement of the 12th of May? Does he know that between the 12th and 13th of May, the UNPROFOR forces entered the Bulevar at the separation line and the third question, do you know that on the 30th of June, after the attack of the BH army at the barracks to the south of Mostar, the Spaniards stopped entering Mostar and they withdrew completely? Does he know about this agreement? Does he know that they came in at the separation line between the 12th and the 13th and remained until the 30th of June? After the attack on the 30th of June, they left Mostar and never came back to the separation line. It seems to me that he has no idea about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally speaking, these are questions which are put during the cross-examination, but on line 20, sentence 20, you mentioned Medjugorje, and I believe you were referring to the 12th of May. And General Petkovic is putting questions to you on that topic. Can you very briefly answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could you perhaps give me -- qualify your statement, rather? We are talking about the 12th of May of what, 1993? What year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the 12th of May 1993. The agreement in Medjugorje that was signed by General Morillon on behalf of UNPROFOR. The UNPROFOR commander. The two sides signed. I signed, General Halilovic, and Mr. Thebault also signed it. Do you know of that agreement signed in Medjugorje on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You arrived in September, I believe, but when you answered a while ago, the question that was put to you, you referred to this Medjugorje agreement. So this was the agreement which was signed on the 12th of May 1993; is that right? Were you aware of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was talking about an agreement which was signed in the Medjugorje barracks with the Madrid Task Force. This must have been in September or beginning of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were not aware of the agreement that was signed on the 12th of May 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't specifically aware of that one. The communication between east and West Mostar in May was free, and I believe it was as from July 1993 when West Mostar was in fact sealed or closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have occasion to refer to this matter at a later stage, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, getting back to the -- I asked you about the detachment that was established in East Mostar, and then you were talking about the patrols on West Mostar, I believe. My next question was this: Did the unit that you were attached to, was it ever able to or did it ever establish a 24 hour presence in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No. Not until we could establish a permanent base there, which I think was established by the month of March, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to tell us why a 24 hour presence was not established before then? Before March 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, we did not have a physical base there, and in the negotiations between the Spanish Battalion and the HVO, we felt that it might be incurring into an unnecessary risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to change things just a little bit. I think while the issue is still fresh. Unless there is objection from my learned friends on the Defence side, I'd propose to show the witness a document that's already in evidence at Exhibit P05571. It's an agreement made in Medjugorje in October of 1993. I believe it's had the agreement that the witness referred to a few moments ago. It's not going to be in the binders, Mr. President. I apologise. I hadn't anticipated this one but if the staff can put it on the screens from e-court, I think that we can work that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I recognise this document is in English. If you want to take a moment, you should see on your screen a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we see it full screen in English, please? It looks to me as though we have the B/C/S version of the document. No. That's not it. Okay. Page 2, please. Okay. That's it. Now, if we could perhaps have that -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to recognise this document? Maybe we could go to the next page as well. It's a bit small.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, rather than taking my time, I'll propose that during the break, we will make some paper copies in all the languages for everyone to look at and we'll come back to this. We'll save time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness. Let's just move then into the documents that we do have here in the courtroom, in the binders, and I'd like to ask you to refer or to take in binder B, Exhibit -- or binder B2, I should say, a document that's at tab 5899. 5899, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise this document, sir? Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: This is an official document of the Madrid Task Force. It's a SITREP, situation report, dated 15 October, 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in the very first paragraph there, there is a reference to mortar shelling in East Mostar, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Indicating that about 54 explosions were heard in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: 54 explosions were heard in that area of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll look at a few more of these but the question is simply, you indicated that as part of in fact in responding to one of the questions from our president, you indicated that as part of its mission, Spanish Battalion was keeping track of the number of mortar explosions or other shelling, I should say. Is that reflected in this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. We -- each patrol counted the number of shellings that occurred in its area, and that is why you see here that there is mention of 54 shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll ask you about this in a few more documents, but did the unit keep track not only of the incoming shelling but the outgoing shelling from the east side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. The Mostar, East Mostar and West Mostar patrols were counting shell explosions in their area, incoming and outgoing, of their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question? Witness, we have seen a number of reports from SpaBat. They were all in Spanish. Could you explain why this one is in English? Is there an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know. I'm looking at the people the report is intended for. Maybe the person intended, the report was intended for, is someone in UNPROFOR but, again, that is not mentioned here so I cannot answer you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, just one last question on this document. We'll see it in others. In terms of the distribution, the intended distribution, of this report, there is a reference, one of the references there is the Jegruta, I probably mispronounced it J-E-G-R-U-T-A. Is that the group or the units that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we may need to just redact that line from the transcript that goes out to the public. I think it could tend to identify the witness as having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could try to be mindful of saying specific bits of information that could tend to identify you publicly, I know it's a bit hard, but...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is in the binder at 5950. And, witness, is this an INTREP number 330 dated the -- appears to be the 20th or the 19th of October 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That's so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to a point here, point number 1, in terms of general situation. And there is a reference to a massive exchange of prisoners. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the report speaks about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then turning to Jablanica, again there is a reference in item 3 to exchange of prisoners continuing throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then finally at the end of the document, in -- under the heading of "other information," item 4, there is some information that tells us why this was called "massive," SpaBat escorting a Red Cross convoy of 14 lorries, about 500 persons from Gabela to Jablanica-Konjic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So is this report indicating or documenting the types of prisoner exchanges that you've mentioned were part of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you briefly just tell us how those were organised? How did you learn about them and what specific responsibilities were carried out by your unit, or I should say the unit that you were attached to, in respect of all of these prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, as I said previously, my mission was to fulfil the order I had received, coordinate the aspects that had entailed, and pass it on to my unit, and of course transport the people and protect the convoys. Now, the prisoner agreement could come as a result of agreement between the parties or by a unilateral decision as well, of one of the parties, or maybe as a result of interposition of the Task Force or international organisations, in some cases primarily the ICRC. I would then arrive at the point of origin. I would escort the ICRC vehicles or whatever vehicles it may be. If the prisoners were going to be conveyed in vehicles, or sometimes if security conditions so required, we would actually drive them, escort the prisoners in our own armoured vehicles. We would then accompany the convoy to the destination which was usually in a secure area, secure for the prisoners who had been freed and then we considered our mission to be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then one final point on this document, I see toward the beginning, there is a reference in the area Mostar East, 15 mortar shells during the night. Again, incoming. And then the next item 2, counting nine "departures" is the word I have in English. So again, is this an indication of the continued counting that the unit was conducting of the incoming and outgoing shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is so. Here, you see that 15 grenades exploded in Eastern Mostar and that also from Eastern Mostar we heard nine outgoing shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there is a note here that three of them landed 300 metres from the patrol. Is that the patrol that was attached to your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: On this date, yes. It would be that patrol. It would probably refer to the place where we had parked our vehicles. When they were in stationary position, and not on actually patrol and moving in the patrol situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next exhibit is 06688, tab 6688. And that is going to be in a different binder, Witness. I apologise. It's going to be in the binder that's marked list A, 6688.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 6688. Do you have that document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then can you tell us, do you recognise this as one of the Spanish Battalion reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is this a situation report for 16th of November 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: 16 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was it normal or customary that reports like this would have been distributed to the unit that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. I am mentioned here as one of the intended recipients of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You said that we are now into November of 1993. You personally, could you tell us how frequently you personally went into East Mostar during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Movements into Eastern Mostar was part of my detachments and the frequency with which I went to Eastern Mostar, unless I had to attend to urgent matters requiring more frequency, but the usual frequency was about on a weekly basis or maybe every five days. That is approximate frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then were you in a position to see for yourself the situation, the humanitarian condition, in East Mostar during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, information in this particular SITREP about the situation in East Mostar, is that information that would have been provided by members of the unit that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. The paragraphs that refer to the situation are produced by that Task Force, and they refer to the situation in Eastern Mostar. Usually the source was the patrol that we had actually detached to Eastern Mostar. Some reports come from the Madrid Task Force or from members of the colonel's staff, and sometimes the colonel would tour the city as well, but generally speaking the reports were produced by my own patrol detached to Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in point 2, Witness, here, there is a reference to the situation Mostar, "In the Muslim quarter is totally pathetic, food and water needed, the city has almost been destroyed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: In point 1 A 2, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that reference. Yes. The situation in Mostar is as you see here in the document. It was a situation where water was lacking, no electricity was available, housing was very damaged, and the bombing was a heavy bombing, as we've seen, and the risk situation was high risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just noticed on the second page, there was reference to severe weather conditions and I wanted to ask you if you could comment on the effect of the coming of winter as we move through November, its effect on the population in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I believe that the difficult living conditions of course were worsened by the cold and the arrival of winter and of course the presence -- there was lack of wood and the houses were damaged. A lot of the window panes were broken. And that of course made the life for Eastern Mostar inhabitants even more differ. At this time there was also some fear that the weather conditions would further hamper the arrival of humanitarian assistance convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit also in the A binder is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Before looking at the next exhibit, Witness, in the last document, I would like you to turn to the end of the document, please, Otras Actividades. And I would like you to look at the middle of this page, where it starts with SpaBat continue [Spanish spoken] and so on and so forth. Do have you that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, are we speaking about the same exhibit, 6688?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Si. Right at the end of the document, under the heading --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do see the reference now, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where one mentions Los Morteros.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in order to avoid shelling or close to hospitals or other sanitary or health protection installations, that means that you should avoid placing military objectives or targets close to such health situations. The Armija was constantly complaining of having bombing near the hospital and the HVO responded that it was countershelling that the Armija had actually effected from the vicinity of the hospital. The Spanish patrol tried to patrol the whole area but more specifically, these areas close to the hospital in order to avoid deployment of Armija mortars in that area which could then justify a shelling response. This was an ongoing permanent situation and that is why I must say that on some occasions we did find mortars actually deployed in the vicinity of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have listened to you carefully. You have just said that you found close to the hospital in East Mostar mortar shells that had been fired, that had been fired by the ABiH or by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I did not explain clearly, sir. On some opportunities, there was shelling by HVO that landed in the vicinity of the hospital, but there was also mortars of the Armija that were used to fire from the proximity of the hospital. These were BiH mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is extremely important. What you are saying is extremely important. You have just said, on line 8, page 32, that according to you, the ABiH had used mortars in the vicinity of the hospital. Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. We conducted surveillance to prevent that from happening, but I also said that on some opportunities we did actually find mortar weapons in that vicinity. I cannot say with what frequency this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you can say that it wasn't a usual situation, that you didn't always find mortars in the vicinity of the hospital, but, rather, something that happened from time to time, occasionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suppose it was from time to time. But when you position a mortar and use it to fire shells, that takes very little time and we were not there on a permanent basis, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to object on the transcript in view of Judge Trechsel's question. I think that in a way it is not for judges even to put capricious questions after the witness provided three answers. I don't think that it was fair, the way the question was put, and I would like that to be on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I do not see what was capricious about that question. It was just a question for the witness to clarify something that he had said. Refuse the protest. I think it's not justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is no need to discuss it. I think that it was a capricious question, and it contained an answer in it. After the witness said the same thing three times, the question was put to him yet again. I don't want any decision to be made by the Trial Chamber on this. All of us heard your question and we reacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it is also necessary to say that in the documentation that was prepared along with this witness, at least in half of the reports, according to my records, it is noted that mortar positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were next to the hospital and that SpaBat tried to remove these mortar positions that were next to the hospital. And also, it is registered in these reports that mortar positions were changed, which is one of the rules in mortar activity, that after firing a few shells, since the enemy can detect the position of the mortar, then they change their positions. Therefore, Judge Trechsel's question was a very symptomatic one, and I believe that the reaction of the Defence is justified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, please proceed. We have ten minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise but now I recognise the problem. Judge Trechsel asked me why do I think that the question was capricious? Because this is the terms as my Croatian was translated. It was wrongly translated. I used a term in Croatian "kapciozno" which in our theory includes -- which in our theory -- which in our theory means leading, because there is a response included in the question. So this word which is here in translation, capricious, is absolutely wrong. Sorry, Judge. It's a misunderstanding on this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm very happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I do think your question was leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I accept that and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, the next exhibit, which is in the same binder, is 6334. And maybe to move it along before the break, can I just ask you does this appear to be something called an operational diary of the Spanish Battalion for the month of November 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative, sir. Yes. This is the operations log of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would like to direct you to two parts of this. The first is at the entry for the 16th of November 1993. And there is a reference in the

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There is a reference here to one of the explosions took place close to the patrol, "Four missiles hit the very same building where the patrol had found refuge." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask to you comment just in general on the extent to which members of the Spanish Battalion were affected, their operations were affected, by shelling from the west side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: In Mostar, the deployment area was rather broad, and as you see, was subject to numerous shell impacts. We were there because we weren't a target for those.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear if we were or were not the target of the explosions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they felt close to us. At that time, in any case, many explosions, grenades, fell very closely to where our vehicles were parked which was the Marshal Tito street. The other reference here concerning an anti-tank shell, I don't know if it was while the patrol was stationary or actually moving during a patrol mission, but in any case, artillery or rifle fire was frequent against us, incoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your answer, we saw that I think the interpreter may have missed a pretty significant part of your answer. So let me ask you to clarify one part. Were you saying that the Spanish Battalion was a target, an intended target, for such action or was it not an intended target, in your view, the view of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Let me correct. On mortar fire I said that we were occupying a zone that was subjected to artillery or mortar fire, and since we were there, obviously it landed near us as well. So we were the object but not the target of that shelling. In the area where our vehicles were parked, Marshal Tito avenue is an area that normally was subject to shelling, many grenades fell there, and that is why I say that there were explosions close by to where our vehicles were parked in that date in November. There is another reference in the same paragraph, mentioning armoured vehicle or shelling, and I don't know if this refers to shell fire landing in the parking lot or if it was shelling against our patrol as it moved through Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can take the break now, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. We are now in open session. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, before we took the break, we were looking at Exhibit P6334 which is the operational diary for November of 1993. I'd like to take you to one other entry in that document, on the 27th of November 1993. And specifically, in the second paragraph of this entry, there is a reference again to perhaps the same Spanish Battalion soldier that we spoke of before the break, relating to an operation or some activity to rescue an injured woman or to get to the place where a woman had been injured. And as the entry continues, there is an indication that the unit encountered sniper fire, and then had to use a smoke bomb to try to get to the woman, who was ultimately transferred to a safe area together with another young woman who was a staff member of UNICEF. So I wanted to ask you if you recall that incident and if you could tell the Trial Chamber what your recollection is of what occurred there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I remember this incident very clearly because this was really a merit of one of my officials and two officials also from my unit but sanitary staff. They told us that there were two wounded women in a street in East Mostar which was being fired by snipers. One of the officers got to the area and he tried to rescue both women, and from the position to which this officer could go to and where the women were, there was an area still fired by snipers and every time they tried to get close to that area, they continued firing. The only solution, therefore, given the nervousness of the women was to try to use a smoke bomb in the area and to have a quick access to where the women were to evacuate them and to take them to hospital. One wasn't wounded and the other one, as the report says, the woman belonging to UNICEF was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to clarify because it indicates at least the English translation that I have indicates that the UNICEF person was not wounded and the other --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry, sorry, I would like to correct myself. Yeah, the woman who wasn't wounded belonged to UNICEF. My error.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall or do you know what positions or the areas from which the sniper fire was coming in this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: From West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next exhibit that I want to take you to is Exhibit P07039, which is in the B binder, 7039.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I should have been doing this before, but a number of these statements or documents are explicitly referred to by the witness in his 92 ter statement, and if you like, I can also mention that this is referenced in paragraph 69 of the witness's Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is an official document from the tactic unit Madrid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The first incident that I want to ask you about here relates to the death of a couple of members of the Spanish Battalion in a mine incident. Do you recall that incident and can you tell us what you recall about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do remember. It is the death of only one officer. The other officer was severely wounded. They were recognising the Dyke of Salakovac when a mine exploded which impacted the captain that -- whose name you can see in the report. And it severely wounded the sergeant that was with him. Another captain from the Chief of Staff of the Task Force tried to help them, and he was also fired, and he had to take shelter in the dike where the accident occurred. He tried to stop the fire, and the patrol that had taken them to the area and was close to the dike went there and that is how we managed to retrieve or to get the body of the captain and the wounded sergeant who was taken to the health unit of our organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this incident is also described in more detail at the end of this same report, under item 5, other information, number 6, which is on page 6 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if you can tell us this Salakovac dam, in general, where was this location? Was it within the area of the HVO or the Armija or neither? There is a reference here to the fire having come from the western slope of the valley, probably from the HVO. So I just wanted to ask you whether this incident can be attributed to any of the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: The report states that the fire seems to come from the area controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there is a -- some ambiguity. I'm looking at paragraph 6 in this report as to the circumstances of the death of Captain Vargas. It's indicated as I see that he is head of the mine clearance team for ordnance. So apparently this officer was the one in charge of the mine-clearing team. My question is this: Did the mine explode while they were doing their work, whilst he was making sure that the mine was no longer active, or was it that he was just passing by when the mine exploded? Could you shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The captain was the chief of the explosive unit and it was during the reconnaissance mission of the mine. When he was there, the mine exploded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And can it happen that members of an explosive team be injured whilst they are doing their work by explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this mine characteristic in any way? It was a mine against -- or land-mine or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anti-person, sir, mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And had it been buried into the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seem to remember that it was on the surface because it was on top of the dam, which was a concrete dam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, the very next paragraph of this report makes a reference to a place called Gabela, sources indicating that a thousand Muslim prisoners are there in very crowded conditions. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: The report gives a statement, the sources are reliable sources, but I can't tell you more than that because I didn't visit the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That was my next question was whether the unit that you were attached to was ever present inside the Gabela facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No, never, never within the prison, as far as I remember. The massive movement or transfer of prisoners that we have mentioned previously, the transfer from Gabela to Jablanica, was carried out using a Red Cross lorries, escorted by a unit that wasn't my unit, because we were in charge of prisoners from Konjic to West Mostar. I don't know whether there was other escorts. I don't know whether my patrol escorted other people there, but it wasn't normal for the units to go to the prison. They collected the people or the convoy at the door of the prison normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few seconds, please. Mr. Registrar, can we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll look into it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you a question about --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to go back to the incident regarding where the clearing of the mine. Mine clearing was a task for SpaBat generally speaking? Was SpaBat in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SpaBat tried to open, as much as possible, all communication lines and all obstacles that we might encounter. Later on, we provided the cleaning of the minefields or the clearing. We organised the clearing and we protected the clearing activities, but it wasn't a specific task of our unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us why, right then, a mine was being cleared in Salakovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we cleared mines in Salakovac and in others areas. We had to clear mines in those areas where we had to go through. For example, close to the ULAU [phoen] when we had to start working there or when we had to start with our reconnaissance operations for technical studies for the reconstruction of the bridge. We had to clear many mines that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, if I could take you now to Exhibit 7293? Same binder. There is reference to this document in paragraph 71 of the witness's statement. Now, witness, this is an INTSUM, intelligence summary, covering the period of 14 to 20 December 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for this case we're really only concerned about the beginning part of it, particularly related to Mostar. Again, here there is a reference to a HVO unilateral release of some 1100 prisoners during this period of time, 15 to 20 December. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it in the Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There is also reference to the evacuation of wounded people and their families from East Mostar to third countries, including Spain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question here is simply this: Can you give us a general description, when prisoners were released from the camps, or were otherwise evacuated with the assistance of the Spanish Battalion, where were they taken in general? Were they free to go back to their homes or were they taken to specific locations that is were you instructed to take them to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I've got to repeat what I've said before. Now, the order that I received to escort, transport, and protect wounded people or prisoners was simply to collect the prisoners or the Red Cross convoy or other organisations' convoy at the point where they were freed and to take them or to escort the convoy to their destination, which normally was an area which was secure for them. Whether there were members of the HVO -- well, if there were members of the HVO, we left them in East Mostar. They didn't need any further protection. So West Mostar, sorry. So that was our mission. We considered our mission fulfilled once we got to the destination point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next Exhibit is 7408?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I thought Mr. Stringer was going to put a follow-up question to you, Witness, but this is important, this issue of the destination for released prisoners is important. Who was instructing you as to that destination? You would take them at a given point in time, you would transport and escort them, but who would tell you they will leave point A to go to point B? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I received on a daily basis the order of the chief of commander, and that doesn't mean that my Task Force had more information. Well, what I -- the information I received was that I had to collect somebody in Rodoc and take them to East Mostar. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you would carry out the order given to you by the colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, Exhibit P7408 is in the binder, same binder.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: INTSUM 472?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct. And this bears the date of 30th of December 1993, at about midnight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, to direct you, Witness, first, to item 2B, 2B, with respect to the situation in East Mostar, again, just to sort of come back to this, we are continuing to count the shelling activity in East and West Mostar here, and that's reflected in this item, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then moving down to item 3 for Jablanica, there is a reference to prisoners released by the HVO from the Gabela prison at this time. Information was that their condition was good. They were taken from Gabela and - maybe I should ask you this, if I didn't already - the location of Gabela in respect of the base where your unit was headquartered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Gabela was at about one kilometre from Dracevo from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then so these prisoners then were moved up to Jablanica, and moving down to the comment then regarding these prisoners, it's noted that these were not prisoners of war but were people who were imprisoned by the HVO at the beginning of the war because of their religion. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that consistent with your own experience or do you have anything you want to add to that in terms of the profile or the nature of the prisoners whom the Spanish Battalion was transporting pursuant to these releases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next exhibit is 7622, which is going to be in the next binder, binder 3 of 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, by our count, I think I've got about 50 minutes left, cinquante, and I'll be able to finish well within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, for 7622, the first document in this new binder, we are now into January of 1994 and we are going to stay in 1994 for the remainder of your direct evidence. First of all, and I mention this because you were asked about the situation, or you were asked -- the president mentioned the various cease-fire agreements, and here in this report, in item 1.1, there is reference to a cease-fire agreed to at the Medjugorje headquarters on the 16th which has not been implemented, and just to follow up on the question of the President, could you give us a comment in general in terms -- in respect of this, the extent to which cease-fire agreements between the parties were respected during the time of your deployment in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I don't recall this agreement, but the agreements that might have been signed in this moment, they didn't have much practical effect until we got to the end of February or March, and then there was a true cease-fire, and the separation of the confrontation lines but there was no practical evidence that the violence and the fire ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, moving down, despite there having been apparently a cease-fire agreement, item 1.2 for Mostar makes reference now to some 90 hits on East Mostar recorded on the 12th of January. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in the following paragraph, there is a reference to HV, that is Croatian army elements, the number increasing especially in Buna and Stolac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. I do see it, but I would like to abide by the first statement I issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand. So the issue regarding HV presence, Croatian army presence, was one that was noted but it was not something that you dealt with in discharging your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No. I don't recall any mission, any -- vis-a-vis the Croatian army and the presence of that army didn't influence -- had no direct influence on the fulfilment of my mission which was to escort and to protect convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next exhibit is P07706. 7706.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Task force Madrid, sorry, INTSUM Task Force Madrid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then taking you, witness, to item 2, 2B for East Mostar, it's indicated there were 55 impacts, and then I want to clarify what follows because I'm looking in the English, it says none discharge. Maybe -- and just so we are perfectly clear on what's being said, could you read in Spanish, what the Spanish -- the original language, document says regarding those 55 impacts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. It says that 55 explosions in East Mostar, and no fire from East Mostar to -- outgoing fire has been observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Because, Mr. President, I think that's a material distinction or clarification that needs to be borne in mind in the English translation. When I read the English translation, I thought it said that there were 55 impacts but that none of the shells had exploded, none had discharged. And so I think the record on that is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, the Spanish text makes it possible to understand better because you have entradas and salidas, so incoming and outgoing, so it is understood that there were 55 falling into East Mostar but that there was no out going fire from east to West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmativeo, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: One of which exploded about 30 metres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: 15 seconds. On that very day, it seems as though there were three Italian journalists that were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually was going to ask the witness to talk a little more about this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There is a reference to an explosion 30 metres from the premises of the patrol base. Now here we are into January, late January 1994. Is this a reference to the more permanent base that the unit was able to secure in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That's right. By then, and I think towards the end of November, we had a house which was known as a blue house in East Mostar, where the patrol, the radio emitter were lodged. The explosions which took place in the vicinity of the house, and here one is mentioned, 30 metres from the house, refers to the actual building of the base, and establishes a difference, two, to place in front of the BMRs, we have the BMRs parked in our usual parking lot, which were by the street, and very close by we have the base. So two impacted near the vehicles and one nearer the base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the record, the BMR, does that correspond to APC, armed personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's exactly the same, APCs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, there is a reference here then in this same paragraph to ten Muslim persons having been killed on that day as a result of the shelling as well as three Italian journalists. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I recall the death of the three journalists, which was some -- unusual East Mostar, and it took place in a courtyard by the parking lot for our vehicles. A grenade hit the courtyard where they were and that's where they died. And this is what I have fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer, you have said ten civilians. I only read persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't -- I think I said ten -- Your Honour, I think the transcript indicates I said ten persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thought I'd heard civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I said civilians I didn't mean to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall at all, can you tell us at all about the ten persons, the Muslim persons, whether they were civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I can add nothing else. I suppose the figure of ten were given to us by the Mostar municipality sources or it's data from hospital, but obviously we did not get to see the ten dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I should ask you, you've now mentioned the blue house where the unit had a sort of a base in East Mostar, as well as a location where the unit parked its vehicles. Can you give us just a general idea of where those places were located, perhaps specifically in relation to the war hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: From north to south, we would come up to the hospital first, then the parking lot for the APCs, and finally our permanent base. Distance to its base and the hospital? Well, five to 700 metres, perhaps, but I dare not say that with any certainty. I really can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to my learned friend Stringer. When we are talking about this, this important issue, it would be important to establish the distance between the parking lot and the bases of the 4th Corps which is mentioned in a sentence in the document that we are talking about, and as well as in a series of other documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, can you answer this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel actually anticipated my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've given us, Witness, the location, I believe, of the permanent base. I guess we can call that the blue house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, also -- I don't know that we got the location if it was a different location where the units' vehicles, like its APCs, where those were parked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the vehicles were parked, takes the blue house and the hospital, to give you two reference points, the vehicles were in fact parked under an arcade on the Marshal Tito street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then finally, in relation to the headquarters of the 4th Corps, where this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Sorry, what are you referring to? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The shelling incident in which the Italian journalists were killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: From the parking lot or from the car park where the vehicles were, you had to cross some houses or a courtyard, courtyard which was pretty close, I'd say, 70 to 80 metres, at the most a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you would arrive at the headquarters of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I'm referring to the courtyard where the death of the three journalists took place. I cannot remember whether it was a courtyard of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The location where the journalists were killed, if I could just be allowed to clarify this, I think we can take care of it without any intervention. Thank you, Mr. President. Could you tell us in general the location of where the journalists were killed, that location in relation to the headquarters of the ABiH 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I would not venture to give you any distances, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next point --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move from that point. I think we've gotten what we can for my purposes. If someone wants to come back to it in cross-examination, obviously they are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just one question because, well, behind the question, there is the problem which the Judges will eventually have to settle. They will have to make decisions in the last instance, at the end of the trial. These ten persons who were killed apparently on the basis of this document, they were killed because of explosions, because of shelling, but the report is not very precise. We do not know exactly where this group of people was. Secondly, we do not know whether the three journalists were part of the group or were separate from the group, because your document says nothing on this. But there is a question to be raised, and Mr. Stringer did try to obtain an answer on this. Were these people in the vicinity of the headquarters? Could you estimate the distance under 100, over 100 metres, under 50 metres, as far as you can remember? I know this goes a long way back. But you said earlier on that the death of these three journalists had remained in your memory. So to know where their bodies were may be able to prompt you to remember what distance there was from there to the headquarters, or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The demise of the three journalists, Your Honour, I have fresh in my mind because unfortunately the death of people in Bosnia was quite frequent, unlike the death of journalists. I remember the three were in a courtyard very close to where we had our vehicles parked. I understand the question by the Prosecutor and the ones that may well come from the Defence counsel, East Mostar is or was a small town and everything was close by us, and the area where shots could come from could be interpreted in very many ways. Hence, I dare not say how close or how far the yard was from the different military objectives. Now I could show you on a map of Mostar where the car park of our vehicles was and where the so-called blue house base was situated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you for your answer. It may be that the Defence will put that in their cross-examination, yes, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to be of assistance but I don't want to be of assistance to the Prosecution. We'll do it during the Defence time. We have this map of Mostar, but we'll come up with an even better map during the cross-examination, but let me say, Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, I have to comments on this. It all seems rather absurd. The Prosecution now here with reference to a detail is trying to prove the killing of ten civilians and three [Realtime transcript read in error "ital January"] Italian journalists. Now, if we were in a classical court of law, I don't have to remind you that, we at the very least would have photographs from the scene of the incident. I know that it might have been difficult to get them, but if the Defence can do this with very limited resources, then the Prosecution should at least have brought in a map and diagram, and the witness said what I was going to say: Give me a map and I'll show you. The witness is a professional officer and he could work with a map. This way, we are wasting ten or 15 minutes of our valuable time trying to determine the location. It's up to the Prosecution. If they wish to have this as an exhibit they should bring in a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just one correction, line 11 it's not ital January, it's three Italians. So you'll have to replace this to have three Italians. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
