utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next point on the -- well, it's on the same page of the English translation at the bottom, there is a reference to a girl who had been wounded in the hip by a sniper. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question here again is incidents such as this, civilians being hit by sniper fire, first of all, was it something that members of your unit encountered regularly during the course of its deployment in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: But, to say that it was something we saw regularly could be interpreted in various ways, since there was so often this took place, but yes, quite frequently we had to respond to requests from civilians from East Mostar so as to pick up the wounded or the dead who had been killed or wounded in areas under sniper fire. Normally, we would go with one or two APCs and attempted to in fact protect the wounded person from further shots so as to evacuate that person to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you say evacuate that person to hospital, is -- would this be to the hospital on the east side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, to the hospital in Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next exhibit is P7771, which is the next document in the binder. This is an intelligence summary number 436 dated the 2nd of February 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, under item 2A for West Mostar, there is a reference here to a Mr. Prlic and a General Kot regarding deployment of UN forces in West Mostar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, so here, by early February, your unit or the unit you were attached to, still did not have any permanent presence in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That's right, we did not have a permanent base there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again, what was the reason for that, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: We did not have the authorisation or rather we did not have a facility, a premises, we did not have premises to have such a base there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, did the Spanish Battalion have the support of the HVO in establishing a military presence in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Obviously not. If we -- we would have wanted to do the same we had done on the other side, but we could not do so until March.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I apologise for interrupting but since the Prosecution is linking his questions to the paragraph in the document that was read out, I would like to ask the witness on the basis of which -- on the basis -- or rather how is that paragraph linked to the question? Was he at the meeting? Does he know about the contents of the meeting, the topics discussed at the meeting, or anything with respect to the meeting at that time, not in July, when the Prosecution showed the witness the document, but when he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can put this in cross-examination. Still, witness, can you answer briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just please interrupt because now the interventions are really coming before I'm actually able to complete the point. I mean they are legitimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you wanted to raise the question, didn't you? Well, put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because what I tried to do in my questions, I believe, is to ask the witness specifically what does he know based on the position he had at the time, and so this is again the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, based on what you know, was the security situation in West Mostar such that it was not possible for members of your unit to be deployed in West Mostar on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it was possible from a security point of view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Lack of safety or insecurity was part of our job. Obviously, it was more perilous for us to be in Eastern Mostar than in Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, what efforts do you know about that were made in order to attempt to establish a permanent Spanish Battalion presence in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: We attempted to do so from our arrival in Bosnia, from the moment we arrived in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you know in what way those attempts were made, how that was handled within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, all this was the duty of the Chief of Staff of our battalion who were the ones that had direct contacts with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this report, there is a reference to a meeting involving Mr. Prlic and General Kot. Do you know if you were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And according to this it was stated that deployment of the UN forces in West Mostar was not considered as appropriate but it was believed to be a useless risk. Is that consistent with the reasonings that you were informed such a presence could not be established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, there was the reason wielded or given, but I don't think it would have been an unnecessary risk for our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, if the HVO was saying it was a useless risk, do you accept that? Or do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I disagree with that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your unit -- the units of -- the units deployed in West Mostar, can you tell us in general what time of day did they arrive and then leave West Mostar? Since they couldn't stay 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: We had a shift system. First thing in the morning we arrived in Mostar, in West Mostar, rather, the patrol stayed there patrolling all morning, came back to the Dracevo detachment for lunch and returned in the afternoon until dusk and stayed there until dusk when they once again returned to the Dracevo headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if their movements, their patrolling activities, were limited within West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, we had problems entering West Mostar. There was a check-point in the Varda area, if I'm not mistaken, and on pretty many occasions, the patrol was not allowed or could not, rather, go into West Mostar and sometimes there were also limitation problems, limitations to the freedom of movement of the patrol in the city. But the major problems were access sometimes to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What about East Mostar? The permanent presence on the east side, were there places that were off limits, that you weren't allowed to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No, no, none, no limitations in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, item 2B relates to East Mostar, 82 explosions were recorded in the city of which 59 took place between the hours of midnight and 1.00 in the morning. And then in the next paragraph, HVO laying mines on the road at the entrance to East Mostar at the area of the airport. You see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then would it have been necessary for the Spanish Battalion personnel to remove those mines if they wanted to pass through this place on their way to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, I'm going to read this paragraph, if you will. We had to cross the airport runways in order to gain access to West Mostar. The mines were not a particular problem because very often they were in fact placed in areas which we did not go over. But if we had to use those tracks then we would clear the mines. But we had basically problems gaining access to West Mostar at the check-points and on the way out, and as I say problems were the rule rather than the exception at check-points. But mines were not a problem. I insist we had clear rules of engagement, and any member of a check-point by himself could put a stop to a 15-vehicle-strong column.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then turning to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, there is a certain contradiction, I fear. In the document, it is said that it is very HVO soldiers who clear the mines. But a little while ago, you stated that you were the ones undertaking that duty. So what's true? One or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about two different cases, Your Honour. We did not clear mines planted with a military objectives. These mines that the report refers to as at other check-points were mines in order to prevent people from going through and we could do nothing about it. The other mines we are referring to, the Salakovac mines or the Bijela bridge mines were planted there in no man's land, so to speak, which made our life difficult, that put at risk the lives of our people, and those are the ones that we cleared. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, witness, just on the next page, page 3 of the English translation, this would be for you again item B3, there is sort of a description again of the shelling incident which had resulted in the death of the three journalists as well as other individuals and the wounding of two SpaBat personnel on the 27th of January. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then the next paragraph says people were -- the streets are deserted, people were running from one place to another for fear of the shelling. Fear among the population has considerably increased. Could you just elaborate, if you can, the effect on the civilian population of this shelling, the frequency of the shelling, and its effect on the civilian population and their movements in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I think that this is stated in the report. Life in Mostar was permanently subjected to this danger, the number of daily explosions were good reason to understand why people were afraid. I must add that people get used to living with such risks and often the streets were crowded and our parking lot where our vehicles were parked was full of children. And this was an added risk when shelling took place. But this fear, and the risk existed, pervaded life in Mostar, particularly at that time when the shelling was very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During the course of your testimony, you've referred to East Mostar as being a rather compact area. We know that there are civilians there. We know there are military objectives there as well. We also know that there was a significant amount of shelling that occurred in the dark, during the night-time hours. So my question is whether you could comment on the use of mortar and other forms of shelling that's directed into an area such as East Mostar. It's -- whether it's appropriate or inappropriate to use such weaponry in an area such as this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, yours is a very thorny question. Are you talking about the accuracy of weapons? Well, the mortar shells are not the most appropriate weapons to use. If we are talking about the rate of action, neither the mortar nor artillery fire are appropriate. Military fire must in fact aim at military objectives. And on the basis of an operation, a military operation, but I would have to issue a value judgement to be able to say why the shelling took place. All I can say is that shelling did take place against East Mostar and it caused civilian deaths. To go beyond this would be to, as I say, issue a value judgement with little information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then I will move to the next exhibit, which is 8099.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please, before you move on to the next exhibit, you could have put a question to the witness on the 5th paragraph; i.e., the fact that the SpaBat had discovered four mortars. Could you read the fourth paragraph witness, please, which starts off with oja [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Today the second part of the field hospital was introduced without any incidents. Nevertheless in the eastern area of the hospital, east SpaBat has discovered four mortars of 81, 82-millimetres, belonging to Armija. Comment: The installation of these is very close to the hospital and may mean a problem for the safety of such hospital in the future. On the subject of safety, the Armija authorities have spread the rumour that this will be in the hands of an east SpaBat patrol. At present the chief of the hospital is Mr. Safet Suljic." End of comment. I do not think that this refers to the permanent hospital of Eastern Mostar but a field hospital that we introduced into Eastern Mostar attempting to set it up in an area where we could deploy it. That hospital was managed by east SpaBat and we actually helped set it up in Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I recall that it was in the eastern area of Mostar, but again I would not actually affirm that in a committed way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't specify the exact location of the hospital, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, the next Exhibit is 8099. And would this be an intelligence summary, 482, dated 20th of March 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So this is reaching the end --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- close to the end of your deployment in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I just want to take to you item 2, indicating that the prisoner exchanges and the releases are still occurring during this latter part of March. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I see that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the unit that you were attached to, was that unit involved in making these prisoner exchanges come to -- was your unit involved in transporting prisoners during these releases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in general, prisoners from Rodoc, those were taken to East Mostar, Jablanica, and also a few to Mostar West?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, an additional question: These prisoners here are all designed as POW. Was that used in a technical sense or was it sort of a routine abbreviation? Was there some verification on their status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the report speaks of POWs and it is -- refers to prisoners of war. There are other reports where civil prisoners are mentioned, or civilian ones, civilian personnel. These are the two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And witness, the next exhibit is in the binder A, number 7763. Now, witness, this one is a little bit different from the other Spanish Battalion documents that we've been looking at. So let me just ask to you take a look at this one, and if you could please tell the Trial Chamber what this one -- what this is, who would have made this report and where it would have been sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: This report is a memo from the officers staff or the chief of our unit, providing information and intelligence. If memory serves correctly, this refers to a document which describes the activities of that part of our detachment, over the four months of last month of 1993 and three first months of 1994, so this document is not intended to the subordinate units but the document is used as a reminder of what has been done and is intended for the higher officer levels, in this case probably intended for the chief of the unit located in Bosnia, and who was then the chief of the unit was based in Spain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just looking through this, it contains a significant amount of detailed information and analysis, would it be fair to say, relating to issues that were beyond your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. This basically constitutes a summary of everything that transpired within our section. Some information pertains to my unit and other information does not. In any case, I was not one of the recipients of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there is one part of this document that is of interest to me, and I hope to others as well, which is the information found in 3 annexes to the report, and I wonder if you can find those, annex 1, annex 2, annex 3. They are graphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document number, the ERN number that would assist would be R 0642624, ending in 2624, 25 and 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, I want to ask you if you recognise this. It's not something that you made but is it based upon information that you know about, that you talked about here in your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I think so. These documents reflect in graphic terms the contents of the daily INTREPs and at the beginning of course it basically indicates the incoming and outgoing shell fire from eastern and Western Mostar. I cannot guarantee the veracity of each of these or the precision, but I would say that the graph is probably what best represents those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this would be -- appear to be a daily day by day graphic representation of the shelling incidents that your unit was recording during their deployment in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, to come back to the Medjugorje Agreement, I think I have a few minutes left and it may be useful. During the break, we made copies of Exhibit P05571, and we have copies to distribute and we need to give one to the witness also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you can disregard the first page of this actually because that's -- page 1 is not relevant for our purposes today but what begins at page 2, you had mentioned earlier, and I know this is in English, you had mentioned earlier an agreement made in Medjugorje during late September or early October of 1993. Is this the document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you involved in implementing or monitoring compliance with this memorandum on cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I did not participate in the drafting of the document, nor in its implementation. But of course, the -- we did of course record the number of incoming or outgoing shell fire from and into Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that the monitoring the shelling activity, was something carried out by the unit you were attached to as part of this agreement? Or you were doing that because -- at least in part because of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is so. In the fulfilment of the orders I received, I considered that a consequence of this agreement was counting the shell fire on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this has come up already, and I'm sure it will come up some more. There is a reference here to location of hospitals and the positioning of military installations in relation to hospitals. So is that why you were monitoring the location of mortars on the east side of the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, we were monitoring and trying to prevent the location of such mortars because there were complaints by HVO and we didn't want such a thing to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then finally going to the signature lines here, there appears to be a signature by the commander of the Madrid Task Force, that's Colonel Carvajal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then also there is a signature over the name of Berislav Pusic. And I wonder if you had any dealings with that person, Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I do not recall. I don't think so. But we may have met at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now 20 past 12.00. It might be a good time to have a break until 2.30. Which Defence counsel will start when we resume?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be us but we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be our turn next. We are going to check our notes and then after the break we are going to tell you whether we intend to cross-examine or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's begin now so that we remain on schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our Defence will consult our clients and after the break we will inform you about our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not making much progress. Mrs. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is the same. I suppose we won't have any questions but we will inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall see what happens after the break. You will have three hours and it is for you to share the time in a way which you deem fit. We shall now have a break and resume at half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.19 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed in open session. We are going to raise the blinds. Just an announcement by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber noted the following: Witness C, who appeared on the 17th and the 18th and the 19th of September, following his appearance, the Prosecution had filed a list of exhibits but it appeared that the registrar did not think at the time of giving an IC number for the said list so we need an IC number. I'm going to give the floor to the registrar in a moment. Should the Defence have any comments, they should do so tomorrow. Mr. Registrar, please, an IC number for the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. One of the parties have submitted list of documents to be tendered through Witness C. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number ICC 677 and several parties also submitted list of documents to be tendered through Witness DV, the witness submitted by the OTP shall be give everyone number IC 678. The list submitted by 4D shall be given IC 679. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now has come the time for the cross-examinations. The Defence teams have had time to prepare themselves. Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Prlic has no questions for this witness either, thank you .

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, The Defence of Mr. Stojic has no questions for this witness either and cedes its time to the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Praljak does have questions for the witness, and with the Court's permission I should like to start off and then General Praljak would like to ask questions himself and I believe that the arguments in favour of that are self-evident. He was there personally while the witness was there, during that same period, he was the commander, and quite obviously he has specific knowledge, technical and other about those matters, especially with respect to Mostar. And with your permission, I would like to start off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He left, General Praljak left Mostar in November, right, in the month of November 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. And we have evidence of that on the 8th of November he left and after that, he has special information, general knowledge and so on, but he wasn't there at the time himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I'm going to ask you a few questions as Defence counsel for General Praljak. My first question is this: Or rather, the first topic I'd like to deal with is this: You and your colleagues, that is to say officers of SpaBat, had a number of direct contacts with Mr. Praljak, and we saw a number of documents here. And in your binder as well as in the binders of other witnesses, we know that you had those contacts. Now, are you aware of the fact that your colleagues also met him, and did you have any contacts yourself with General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I didn't have any contact with General Praljak. And I know that members of the Madrid Task Force, including my colonel, had contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, to your knowledge, SpaBat as an institution, did it know of his precise function and position in the field within the ranks of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Through those contacts and discussions, did SpaBat know that Mr. Praljak was born and brought up in Herzegovina, specifically in the Capljina area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I cannot answer the questions because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. Witness, in October 1993, General Praljak's father died in that same area, in Grabovine. He lives in Grabovine, near Capljina. Now, do you perhaps remember anything about the funeral or the condolences expressed by SpaBat to the general with respect to his father's death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar help me out, or rather, the usher, and help the witness out with the documents? I think he received a binder like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you look at the first document in that binder? It is 3D 01088. It's the first document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, the Prosecution has not been supplied with any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, they remain on my table but the list was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We don't have a list, Mr. President. But it's okay. I don't see any reason to pause. Except if I might add, Mr. President, I'm looking at the witness's binders which have tabs on them with the numbers, and I'm looking at mine, which don't have tabs. I don't know if anyone else has tabs or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last time, Mr. Kovacic, we had said that just out of courtesy, the Defence could try to put in tabs for the Prosecutor, and he would do the same for the Defence teams. Because, look, it's going to force him to go through, to leaf through the documents, to find them. So, please add some tabs. It's not that much extra work, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, first of all I forgot to place it on my learned friend's table. We didn't do that on time, but the list must have reached him. There must be a technical mistake somewhere. As regards the tabs, we really do try and do it whenever we have time. This time I see there are no tabs. You know what our schedule was. We finished one witness yesterday and had overnight to complete this binder, and quite obviously my staff didn't have time to do that. But as you requested this earlier on, although we haven't got any colour, each document which is already an exhibit states an exhibit on the tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now Witness, I don't know if you've had a chance to look at the first document on the binder, 3D --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I propose that we take a five minute break so that we can get tabs on this. I'm not willing to sit through a cross-examination struggling to find the documents as counsel leads the witness to them. So I'm proposing a five-minute break so that I can get tabs, and I'll do it myself or with the assistance of Ms. Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber is going to give you one of their batches of documents in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we are going to take the documents that had been given to you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one, too, with the tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I hope you've had a chance to look at the first document now, it is 3D 01088. Have you managed to look through it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I can see it, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you turn to -- it's just the first document. I think you've gone on further. This is what it looks like, just a short document, Witness. That's right. [In English] That's it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This, then, is a telegram or probably it was sent by fax, signed by I won't say the name, you can see it yourself, so that we can stay in open session. It is the commander you mention. And you have the translation of it in English on the next page. It is an expression of condolences which your commander sent to my client, General Praljak. Do you agree that that is indeed his signature and that is in fact a SpaBat document, what SpaBat documents usually look like, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you were distributed in different locations, did this remind you, perhaps, or do you know that two officers, as representatives of SpaBat, attended the funeral of General Praljak's father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'd like to move on to another area now. Now, in the Prosecution binders, the documents you've been looking at so far, look at 06518, please. It's an INTREP 350 of the 8th of November 1993. It says, "General state," the second section is "Mostar," and in the section under Mostar we have point 1 and point 2 and I'd like to draw your attention to that point 2. And it says that there was security provided for someone who was held at a check-point at Zitomislici [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry, I can't find the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Binder B2, B2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In point 2, as I was saying, it says that "SpaBat patrol was kept at Zitomislici in spite of the letter signed by General Praljak, the HVO commander, which was received yesterday at SpaBat headquarters." Have you found that, Witness? [In English] Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then another section, a comment, it says comment, and it says, "Once again we have seen how little or not at all the commanders of the HVO -- how much power they have, how little power they have over the terrain, little or no power." You're a professional soldier, Witness. You are a high-ranking officer. You were in Bosnia. Now, in your preparations for taking up your mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially since one of your battalions was there before you, did you learn about the circumstances in which the military wing of the HVO was established? What were the circumstances and conditions, in general terms? Did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No. I don't really know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As observers, and it was your role to be an observer among other things, do you know that the HVO was not formed, or, rather, did not act there like some earlier established army with its structure, training, and so on? That's not how it came into being. But it was established when the Serb army launched an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and then people took the initiative to self-organise and that's how the HVO came into being and was established. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you accept that on the basis of the prevailing conditions, this was an army rapidly formed and organised, which functioned in the best way that the circumstances allowed it to and developed as it progressed, in fighting the Serbs and later on in the conflict with the Muslims, it became organised to the best of its ability under the circumstances and given the conditions that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My objection is I don't think this witness is not competent to give an assessment since he was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina until September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic, you're asking questions of this witness as to the way the HVO was created, to meet the aggression by the Serbian army whilst the witness was not in the field. Witness, can you answer this question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not with any accuracy, Your Honour. Our units were not present whilst the conflict with the Serbs was raging, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I'll drop some of my next questions in view of your position. However, I would like to remind the Court that a group -- the Canarias group was there from the beginning of the conflict with the Muslims, and the previous witness said that they had been briefed about the events that took place prior to their arrival, so they didn't arrive there with blank knowledge, with a tabula rasa, so that was the position. And I'm bearing in mind the fact that of course the witness is an experienced and well-trained soldier, and he was in the field and that was quite obvious, and I think that any soldier would be able to observe that. But I have received an answer so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, witness, would you look at the next document, 3D 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To assist the Defence, perhaps one could ask the witness whether he observed professional or highly unprofessional behaviour on behalf of the HVO, whether it gave the impression of an army which works well or generally which an amateurish -- something amateurish. I hope this would be in the sense of what you are aiming at, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that suggestion, Your Honour. I was getting to that by first asking the witness about the time when the HVO was established but perhaps I could go more directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard Judge Trechsel's proposal. Now, while you were there, what were your impressions? Was the HVO well-organised a well-structured army with a firm chain of command in place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: As you well know, we do not participate in the actual conflict. We were not, in fact, intervention forces or interposition forces, and we were not in fact in touch with the HVO command or the Armija command. My first contacts had to do with the check-points or those troops managing communication lines. I suppose I could say that the behaviour and presence of the HVO troops present was not up to the expectations of a professional army behaviour. However, when we, in fact, through our chain of command, made a protest known either because we'd been stopped at a check-point, the organisation finally made this known to the HVO command. So there was some sort of chain of command. However, I'm not familiar with the internal discipline measures taken by those groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One small technical detail, Witness. If you were stopped at a check-point, as you just said, the soldiers manning it, were they in whatever kind of connection with authorities by walkie-talkie or through other ways? Did they have means of communications, making it possible to find an immediate solution to a problem by calling the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We communicated this via our own means of communication and through our own chain of command. When a patrol was stopped at check-point, through our own chain of command, through our own battalion's chain of command, we actually made our problem known, and the task force through the liaison officers made this known to the HVO, and when it arrived there, of course, the HVO command made this known to the lower ranks in order to try to solve the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was more focused. I wanted to know whether the HVO soldiers on the ground were able to communicate with their own chain of command, through radio, walkie-talkie, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that normally they did have some means of communication. I cannot say so for certain at all times, but in very many opportunities, communications did arrive to try to solve the situations. Now, I cannot know whether this was a permanent means of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd like to round off that area, but just to go back to a Prosecution document or rather your statement of the 8th of November, 50618, 06518, do you accept the contents of the statement and the assessment made here? 6518, P06518. We looked at that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Item 2, West Mostar, paragraph 2, you're asking me about my comment about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the comment. Now, do you agree what it says here is correctly stated, everything in the document, including this second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Well, I would not rule out any HVO authorities. In another SITREP, allusion is made to this, I believe. Now, to go to the nutshell, this happened because I believe there was a letter from General Praljak in which he commits himself to ensuring that the VIP convoys would not be detained at check-points for over 15 minutes. However, in this case, the patrol was stopped for over 40 minutes. Hence, the comment. I said before that I'm convinced, and I do believe that the HVO did not, in fact, abide by the standards of a professional army. Nevertheless, I would not say that the HVO chain of command had no authority whatsoever over their troops. That is my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the interpretation wasn't right. I was told that the commander didn't have authorisation over its soldiers. Did you mean to say that it did not have full control over its soldiers, authority over its soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No, no, no. I say that in the HVO units or at the check-points with which we had to deal with, if I had to make a general statement, I would say that they were submitted or subjected to the HVO military authorities, but in the situation we were living in, any isolated soldier, unarmed, was able to stop a 15-APC convoy by himself. However, this does not mean that these people were not subjected to the HVO chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you said contradictory things because initially I was under the impression that your impression was that the chain, the HVO chain of command did not have any authority over the soldiers on the ground. That was my first understanding. Could you be more specific because this is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, either I do not explain myself properly or perhaps the translation has been misleading. I do understand your question. I understand that you're asking me whether I agree or not that the HVO units were units that could act beyond the chain of command of the HVO chain of command, and that is not my perception. I believe that they did act abiding by the HVO chain of command. A different kettle of fish is the following: In those units which did not abide by the standards of a professional army, there may have been more or less discipline or uncontrolled elements, which would lead those people to stopping a convoy in which there were elements unfriendly to them, including perhaps UNPROFOR elements. But in the long run the orders issued by the chain of command were in fact implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your assistance and I'd like to cede the floor to my client. I don't think I need go on any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I've -- I'm just going to take a moment to get myself organised. Good afternoon, Witness. That's how I have to refer to you. I don't -- I mustn't use your rank. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm going to stick to technical matters once again and be as expeditious as possible. Sir, I'm going to ask short questions in the military manner, precise, because of our time constraints. So I'd like to ask you to give me brief answers in the same manner as well. Thank you. Some things have remained unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did leave the area on the 9th of November 1993. That is true. Early in the morning. But for continuity's sake with regard to mortars I'm going to refer to certain documents in order to show the continuity of certain events and actions of the BH army. So I will deal with some documents that are not within that date. With your permission I'd like to use them, and I'd like to clarify something straight away, something that the Prosecution said. It relates to P07706, that document, and it refers to the death of the Italian journalists. Could this map be displayed somewhere, please? We are going to have this map displayed, if we may, to clarify matters still further. And we can take a look at 3D 01071 as well. It's the map in e-court, 3D 01070. It's the map of Mostar which we've seen many times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, we're just going to pinpoint some basic facts on the map. One of them is where the hospital was in East Mostar, the military hospital there, and where the blue building was situated, which was where your headquarters were later on that you mention, 3D 01071. It's not this at all. It's a map of Mostar that we need to be looking at. Well, that map is much bigger than this area but, well, you can still see. Please, 3D 01071 on e-court. Could you please bring it closer to the witness? Would you please bring it closer to the witness? Could you please look at this on e-court? Why haven't we got it on e-court? Sir, sir, Witness, let us clarify that particular detail, when you say that it is a fact that a woman got killed and that a woman from the UNHCR was attacked, and that they were targeted by sniper fire coming from the western side. My next question: At that moment, were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Are you asking me if I was there on the day that we removed those two women from the theatre of operations? No, I was not there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the next day, were you there to have a look at what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I do not recall whether I was there or not. That fact in any case did not require my place on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I'm just asking whether you know that this happened in a very small street that goes to the north of the street of Marshal Tito and is near the national theatre in Mostar. Do you know that, a very small street, a bit to the north of Marshal Tito street, near the theatre in Mostar? I marked it on the map. I put a circle there. Would you please look at the map and tell me the following: On the basis of this report, these women were lying in this ditch. They were being shot at from the west side, as is stated there. My question is: In the previous report, it also says that the street was so narrow that an APC could not enter it. So there are houses around it and the rest. Did anybody take a look, and did you ask as to whether, from the place where they were lying in the ditch, one can see any HVO position, and how far away is that HVO position from that particular place? I marked it on the map. I marked the separation line. You can have a look at that. You are quite familiar with that separation line. So did anybody have a look? There were two ladies lying in the ditch, there are houses around, an APC could not enter that street, and somebody is shooting at them. Did anybody take a look at it in that way? Do you know about that? If not, then I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: General, I cannot provide you with such specific details. I do know that it was a narrow street. I know that the APCs were not able to climb up that street, and I know that the two officers who rescued the women had to cross over an area that was covered by a sniper, in a street that was heading for the western part of Mostar and that these two officers were fired upon when they attempted to rescue the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I fully understand that. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you the following. From that particular place to the west, how many more hundreds of metres are there or kilometres of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? So if we look westward, how many hundreds of metres or kilometres are there until HVO positions start, on the assumption that you can even see it from a house, from there? Look at the separation line on this map that goes along the Bulevar. Perhaps it's going to be easier for you to see on the big map. Unfortunately this one is very small. Perhaps if we could zoom in on this map, then you could see better, the part that is above the old bridge, the middle, a bit further up, a bit further up, could you scroll up a bit? All right, all right. Now, could you please take a look at this here? I have marked this. Now, where is this? It should be turned around, actually. Ah, yes. Now, look at this white dot. That's the national theatre. Further up to the left, do you see this street of Marshal Tito going to the left of the railway station, and then it goes further on, and then we get further up north to this white stain, as it were, which is the building of the national theatre? Do you see that? Can you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: No, I do not see it, if you are actually pointing at it, I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, how do I do this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if it's scrolled up a bit or rather if we look --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness would have to get closer to the parts where Mostar is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the map be lifted up a bit so the witness can see better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a paper map which I think is better than the one on the screen. The problem is if the witness starts to move around then his face distortion is at risk, and so I don't know if there is a way to accommodate those two things. But I think everyone agrees it would be better if somehow the witness could work off of this paper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, quite simply I think that without a map and without the distances involved, the buildings, and then the HVO building on the other side, I mean without all of that we really cannot see from which place one can shoot in a narrow street that is surrounded by houses and two women are lying in the ditch and fire is opened at two officers of the Spanish Battalion too. Please take a look. There is a circle in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness can you have a look, can you recognise any of that? Unfortunately I didn't want to mark it with --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Sorry, are you speaking about these circles here?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, we've got these circles there. Let's move from left to right. The first one I put there is where the Mostar hospital is, the military hospital of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the first circle. Is that correctly marked there underneath the railway station in Marshal Tito street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine it, but the map is of such a scale that it's very difficult to be precise in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. The next mark that I put is the blue building where you were, the former Energoinvest Hotel that is very close to the military hospital of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Between your building and the military hospital, you parked your cars; is that right, in a particular area? The third mark there is -- in response to my question, whether between the blue building, which is the second mark, and the military hospital, there was a parking lot where you left your cars, parked your cars, what was your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes. I said before -- please just give me a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Spanish translation coming over channel 4] [In English] cannot recognise anything on this map. So we are completely lost and we do not want to you think we can follow if we cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, I quite understand but you see, I think that the trial should have been adjusted in terms of establishing precise facts, accurate facts, very important facts. I'm going to get to that later. First of all, there was a war going on and we are going to get to that through the documents. Someone is constantly keeping mortars by the hospital. There are 20 documents that I will show. Then the command of the 41st command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is among the population. The command of the 4th corps is among the population. Then the command of the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is among the population. Among the population. Right in the middle of town. That parts of the army that deal with logistics are in the centre of town. Your Honour, Judge Trechsel we are in the middle of a war, we are not on a picnic and the gentlemen sitting opposite us, I mean, really, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on the screen which is in front of you, the markings on the larger map, with the markings on the larger map, could you show us where the blue building is, where the hospital is, and so on and so forth? Don't show this to us on the large map. Show it to us on the map which you have on your screen, because I would like you to mark 1, 2, and 3 on this map, please, with the electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, would you start from the railway station that you can see and then please mark the hospital with a 1, 2 blue building, 3, the command of the 41st brigade, 4 the command of the 4th corps, and 5 where the incident occurred, the one that had to do with the two ladies that were shot at, as I marked this there, and then you can testify as to whether that is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I not think that I'm able on such a scale to actually indicate these points. I think that the way General Praljak marked them is probably correct. I have nothing to say about that. And as I said before, our own patrol headquarters was located some 500 metres from the military hospital, and I said that between our patrol base and the military hospital, we had a parking lot for our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I shall try and help you. Do you see where the military hospital is on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir, I do not see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be enlarged, please? Can it be enlarged a bit? And Mr. Pusic who is disabled and who is from Mostar, can he assist the gentleman, or actually let's try to do this in a simpler way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, look at the big map according to information accessible to you. On the big map did I correctly mark the military hospital under A; and then B, the position of the blue building where you were; C, the position of the command of the 41st brigade; and D, the position of the command of the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? 1, 2, 3, 4, all of that is in the street of Marshal Tito.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I see the points on the map, but I don't see any letters nor any numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: From the left to the right, that is how I refer to them. If you agree that all of that is the street of Marshal Tito, was that the way it was, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you now please look at the last dot on the right? There is this little circle next to the big white mark where the incident involving the two ladies happened. Could you put a line there from that dot to the Bulevar where the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO are, westward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I said before that I am not aware of the details pertaining to this incident with the two ladies. I don't even know the name of the street or even where it's located. I do not know these details. Therefore, I cannot say whether the incident took place there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I fully understand you. Thank you. That will do, as far as I'm concerned. Since you testified that my markings are correct --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honour, Mr. President, can an IC number be assigned to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption but I don't know that the witness testified that Mr. Praljak's markings were correct. What I heard was the witness say that he agreed that the Marshal Tito street was correctly indicated, but I don't know that he's agreed that the other locations are correctly marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the general has indicated four locations on Marshal Tito street, A, B, C, and D. In light of these markings on the map, can you confirm A that this is Marshal Tito street, and, B, that these locations are the ones that were mentioned? In other words, that D is where the command of the 4th Corps was located? So far as we do have the letters on the map, but Mr. Praljak seemed to say that we had these letters, A, B, C and D on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't really put any letters. I just marked the hospital, the blue building, the command of the 41st Brigade, and the command of the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is that correctly marked from left to right, these four dots, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, there are four circles from left to right. The first circle is where the hospital is, the second circle is where the blue house is. Third circle is where the command of the 41st Brigade is, and fourth circle is where the command of the 4th Corps is. We have four circles. Can you confirm that these four circles are on those locations which were mentioned by General Praljak, or do you say that you can't recognise these locations? In that case we shall move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that. I do think that that is Marshal Tito street. I think that this mention from left to right on the map corresponds to the hospital, to the parking lot, to the blue house, and to the headquarters and I -- that more or less, I believe that they are present there in the order that the general indicated on the map. I cannot be more precise when looking at things at this scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak would like to have an IC number for this map. Registrar, can we have an IC number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document shall be given Exhibit number IC 680. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, could we just clarify one more thing? Namely, the death of one of your men, one of your men who was killed by a land-mine. Is it correct, sir, that you went there at the request of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that that location where you were is at the Salakovac dam at the exit out of the tunnel on the road between Sarajevo and Mostar? You were asked by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to come there to that dam and then one of your officers stepped on a land-mine there and got killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that interpretation. It could be possible. The person doing the reconnaissance for the dam was the chief of deactivation or mine clearing or explosives clearing, and it's very possible that the Armija may have detected presence of a mine close to the dam and that that was -- that they were present there but that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, witness there seems to be a contradiction now. Now you have been asked whether the officer stepped on the mine. And you said yes, possibly. This morning, you have been asked whether the soldier was killed while trying to disactivate the mine, which is something quite different. Can you say whether one is correct or the other or whether you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was saying, in answer to General Praljak's question, when he said that the Armija had requested the patrol to respond to the dam, and I said yes. That's what I was answering to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are not confirming that the soldier stepped on the mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not confirming that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, why do you say that the Spanish soldier stepped on the mine? This morning, things seemed pretty clear. We said that this man got killed whilst trying to neutralise --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I withdraw that. Actually what I was -- well, I just wanted to ask whether the Spanish team went there at the request of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then, well, I got an answer so I don't want to deal with it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, now that we have dealt with that, I would like to go back to the question of the Croatian army. In your first statement, you said, or rather can we have 3D 01090 on our screens? 3D 01090. Witness, you have that in my binder, page 3. Take a look at this. It's like this. You see, this kind of document. Or, rather, it was already prepared for the gentleman who came here before you, but I didn't manage to use it until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? Witness it's the second binder, the smaller one, DV.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I don't think I have the second binder that's being referred to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yesterday's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You got it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't get it yesterday because I wasn't here yesterday and my colleague, Mr. Poryvaev, who was here yesterday, was never alerted, nor was I, that we would need to have a different binder for a different witness present in the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm go to provide my learned friend with our copy. We perceive the Prosecutor's Office as an institution rather than just a collection of people or persons. I apologise for the scribblings on my copy, but I hope it won't bother my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at 3D 01090 and please look at the second page, the part that concerns the arrows, to show how the operations evolved against Croatia from Bosnia and Hercegovina. My question is very simple. At the time when you were there, in your statement you stated clearly that at that time, you personally did not see or have information about the Croatian army being deployed in that area. Is that correct? Is that what you stated in your first statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, you're a professional soldier. I'm sure that you got yourself familiar with the general area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you familiar with the following fact, the Croatian army could not reach Dubrovnik in order to defend Dubrovnik from an attack of the Serbian and Montenegrin army without crossing through the territory of Neum which belonged to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were you aware of that fact at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were you also aware of the fact at the time that the Croatian Defence Council that was supposed to defend the area in front of Neum; i.e., the northern part of the territory of Neum -- Neum could not reach those positions without crossing the Republic of Croatia Metkovic, and part of Neum to reach the northern part of Neum, that's how the roads look in the area. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I don't quite know what it is that you're asking me, sir. What do you mean whether I was aware of that at the time? I was not aware that HVO wished to do what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes. I'm asking. I'm asking you if you know it okay. If you don't, never mind. My question is clear. In order to reach the northern part of the defence of Neum, the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, the HVO had to pass through Metkovic, through Neum and reach the hill tops. There was no road there. Do you know it or do you not know it? This my question. If you don't we will clarify that with another witness. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to you ask the question more clearly because I am not able to get the sense of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The south of Croatia looks like this. First there is Croatian territory, then it is intersected by the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where Bosnia-Herzegovina has its exit to the sea, and then the Croatian territory continues towards Dubrovnik. You can see it on the map, below Ploce, you can see it and the situation during the war was this: If the Croatian army wanted to defend Dubrovnik, you testified to that effect, they had to go through Neum because that was the only road, through the hills, and if the HVO wanted to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina territory from the Serbian army, there was no other road for them to reach that area but to go through Metkovic, and then to Neum. And then they have to reach to the Bosnia-Herzegovinian territory in the north and again, the -- a part of the Croatian territory continues after that and the Croatian army had to go through Dracevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is somewhat lost. We have three maps in front of us, and we find it difficult to follow what you are talking about. We have the second map which is a political map relating to 1991-1992. I'm translating from your language because we don't have an English version here. What are you getting at? Because the witness wasn't there at the time. So if you put him a question of a general nature, in that case, ask him to agree with or disprove your theory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the situation is very simple. I have shown the witness the second map. The situation in 1992-1993 did not change, the army of Republika Srpska continued to attack. The Croatian territory, as you well know, is intersected or it is cut near Neum by the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In its continental part, Croatia is cut in one part by the Bosnia-Herzegovinian corridor to the sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second map, the second map, the first or the second map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, Dracevo, was it on the very border between Croatian and Bosnia-Herzegovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina but on the very border maybe a kilometre or two away from the border? Would that be correct? You were in Dracevo. Thank you very much. Unfortunately again for technical problems my following question is this: From Dracevo, did you say affirmativo that Dracevo was a kilometre to two kilometres from the border with Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Between one and five kilometres, I'd say, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well then, very well. My question is this: From Dracevo towards the south, Metkovic to the south, this is where the territory of Croatian state continues; is that correct? To the north is Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the south is Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is this, if the Croatian army is supposed to defend its territory, the coastal part, the only road that could bring them to that area would go through Dracevo. Would it then be logical that the road through Dracevo and the Croatian army would get into the territory that is its territory, wouldn't that be logical, wouldn't that be militarily logical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: It could have some logic, Your Honour. I'd rather be questioned on my statement or on the -- what I've said, but not on the geopolitical or strategic situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're quite right. But from what I understand, from Mr. Praljak, we have a map on which we can see Dubrovnik, and he is saying that if the Croatian army wishes to reinforce the army or go to Dubrovnik, they need to go through Dracevo, a settlement where you were, which might explain - but this is not what he said, I'm just trying to understand what he is demonstrating - which might explain why you, the SpaBat, would have seen members of the Croatian army. Is this logical or illogical? I don't know. What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never studied how a military operation could be conducted so that from Mostar or the southern part of Bosnia it would be possible to go to Dubrovnik. Therefore, I cannot answer you sir. I can speak to you about the roads that I see on a map. Yes there's a road from Metkovic-Dubrovnik indeed, but I cannot tell you that a military operation can or cannot be conducted by following that road or not following that road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Unfortunately I will have to clarify this issue with somebody else in another way. Just for the record I would like to invoke the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement on allowing the Croatian army to enter the areas around the border within the tactical operations. This agreement was signed in 1992. The Trial Chamber has already seen it. Can you now please look at the document P05210? The date is 19 September 1993. We will go quickly through all of the documents that we still have left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: My apologies, general, what folder are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's binder. This is the Prosecutor's document number P05210. P05210. You've already seen it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: This is an INTREP of the Task Force, of the Madrid Task Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 1.1 where it says axis, we had two axes here: The main axis, Metkovic-Mostar, Jablanica, Tarcin, Kresevo, nothing to report; and the alternative route across Dreznica. Did you have two axes towards the north? Metkovic, Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic was the main route or axis across the hill tops, across, Dreznica was the second route, is it correct that there were two routes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: Affirmative, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us now look at the second page of the same document, under Mostar, it is stated that 20 shells fell on the Muslim neighbourhood. Can you see that? Can you just confirm for me that it is stated so herein? Is it correct that this is what is written in this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: That is what it says here, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Under item 2, one SpaBat patrol reported on the fact that the HVO military police forced a group of fighters to return to their positions on the front line. Can you see that? I'm just going to read through the document, and I just want you to confirm that this is correct. Remarks, it is clear that both parties breached the cease-fire agreement, although the level of activities decreased from the moment when the agreement was initiated, that is that. In the text where it says fighting, it says in the report, according to the BiH sources, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the fighting continued in the territory of Trvi [phoen]. They captured 72 HVO soldiers, including the chief of staff himself, and it says here also that according to the same sources, the army isolated the area of Slatina from the area of Prozor. Further on, other information of interest, it says here, according to the BiH sources, the territory of Dreznica and Vernik at the moment does not fall under the responsibility of either the 4th or the 6th Corps of the BiH army. It is directly subordinated to Halilovic. Under item 3, in the same part, it says the same sources report that the operations in the territory of Vrdi and Slatina are going as envisaged. And then in the remarks of this document, it says that the concentration of the HVO troops in Gradina might mean that they were preparing for a counterattack against Vrdi, or they were creating a defence line in order to prevent the advancement of the BiH army to the south. Have I read out everything correctly? Can you confirm, sir, that the document states what I have just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DW
utterances.text: You have read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Praljak, you have now done what the Defence always also criticises. You have a document, you read a part of it. You ask the witness is this written here? But that is not witness testimony. Everyone can read this who can read. You should ask him a question and not just what's in the document, because we all can read that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, of course I'm going to put the witness questions at the end, and I'm going to tell you immediately what these questions are going to be. I'm going to ask the gentleman where they are; I'm going to show him the map. I'm going to ask him how far Vrdi is from Mostar Bijela. I'm going to ask him whether such attacks, according to his information, are part of the offensive of the BiH army that was known under the name of Neretva 93. I simply have to show him the documents first and read them out to him and then put some general questions. Maybe you can give him some instruction as to what to do, but I first have to go through the documents because the Prosecution extracted from the documents only those parts that do not reflect the whole truth. I have to ask the gentleman at the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak is talking about what he's going to do. I'll take the opportunity to tell the Trial Chamber what I'm going to do. When those questions come the objection will be that those issues the operation at this location, Vrdi, the time frame is all beyond the scope thereof witness's direct examination.
